pnwChanterelle576.title: Pilz, Norvell, Danell & Molina 2003, PNW-GTR-576: Ecology and management of commercially harvested chanterelle mushrooms
supports: Cantharellus formosus is the scientific name for the common Pacific golden chanterelle of the Pacific Northwest and Cantharellus cibarius is the European species
Pacific golden chanterelle collections under hemlock, Douglas-fir and spruce; fruits midsummer through late fall in young to old forests
Cantharellus subalbidus is apparently mycorrhizal with Douglas-fir and hemlocks and fruits late summer to early fall in mature to old coastal and montane forests
the Pacific Northwest winter craterelle was given the provisional name Craterellus neotubaeformis nom. prov. because Dahlman et al. 2000 separated it from the European Craterellus tubaeformis
winter craterelles are common in moist conifer rain forests from Alaska to northern California and generally fruit November to May, usually on well-decayed wood or near living roots and stumps
rain during primordia formation allows chanterelle fruitbodies to continue growing without drying (Reijnders 1963, cited)
doesNotSupport: numeric rainfall or soil-temperature thresholds for any Pacific Northwest chanterelle
a published fruiting calendar curve; the calendar described in the source is qualitative

pnwMatsutake412.title: PNW-GTR-412: Ecology and management of the commercially harvested American matsutake mushroom
supports: in central Washington and Oregon the American matsutake most often occurs in mixed conifer stands containing Douglas-fir and western hemlock, and fruits more abundantly in mixed Douglas-fir/western hemlock stands
other reported associates include Pacific silver fir, noble fir, grand fir, Engelmann spruce, lodgepole pine, western white pine and ponderosa pine
Pacific Northwest fruiting typically occurs from 300 to 1200 m elevation
Pacific Northwest harvest runs from late August through mid-November, progressing north to south, high to low and inland to coastal
soils are described as warm, well to moderately well drained sandy/loamy soils with gravel, often glacial till or tephra
fruiting bodies begin to develop when soil temperature falls below 19 C and fruiting typically ceases below 10 C (Japanese shiro studies cited in the report)
stand age matters in managed Japanese pine plantations (pines 40-50 years old described as best)
doesNotSupport: a western North American T. murrillianum thermal curve; the temperature statements are from Japanese T. matsutake shiro work
numeric drainage class or available-water responses

matsutakeTrudell2017.title: Trudell, Xu, Saar & Justo 2017, Mycologia 109: North American matsutake: names clarified and a new species described
supports: three matsutake species occur in North America: Tricholoma magnivelare (eastern USA and Canada), T. murrillianum (western USA and Canada) and T. mesoamericanum (Mexico, newly described)
molecular, geographical and morphological evidence separates the western species from the eastern one

trappe2004Craterellus.title: Trappe 2004, Mycologia 96:498-509: Habitat and host associations of Craterellus tubaeformis in northwestern Oregon
supports: occurrence in northwestern Oregon is highly correlated with the presence of western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) and the mycorrhizal association was confirmed
the species can also form mycorrhizae with Douglas-fir and Sitka spruce but is rarely encountered in stands without a hemlock component
well-decayed coarse woody debris was the substratum for 88 percent of sporocarps
stand age and well-decayed coarse woody debris volume were significantly related to the probability of occurrence
slope, elevation and aspect were not related to occurrence or standing crop biomass
western North American, eastern North American and European populations differ genetically, suggesting several distinct species

Pacific Northwest profile reuses the same sourced prior-year fire response with a May-June engineering calendar and a spring moisture band; no PNW-specific published phenology or severity response exists, so transferability is an inference
candidates.evidenceGapRule: The target declares requiresDisturbance with an explicit evidenceGapCap. When the fire layer is unavailable or no mapped perimeter applies, the disturbance component stays missing, confidence drops, the band states that fire evidence is unavailable, and the score is capped. Absence of a mapped perimeter is never scored as a negative signal.
missing: a per-fire severity response (MTBS publishes no per-perimeter severity class, so severity stays null and applies no penalty)

Taxonomy resolved by Trudell et al. 2017: the western USA/Canada species is T. murrillianum, distinct from eastern T. magnivelare and Mexican T. mesoamericanum. PNW-GTR-412 supplies host associations, elevation, season and soil descriptions.
modelUses: mapped Douglas-fir and hemlock/Sitka-spruce host classes weighted highest, with lodgepole, fir/spruce/mountain-hemlock and ponderosa lower (source-supported hosts, engineering weights)
300-1200 m elevation band read from PNW-GTR-412 with an engineering soft falloff
September-November calendar from the reported late-August-to-mid-November Pacific Northwest harvest (engineering band)
autumn wet-up transition metric and maritime 14-day rain band (engineering)
50-66 F soil-temperature band inferred from the Japanese shiro initiation/cessation temperatures cited in PNW-GTR-412 (explicitly provisional analogy)
candidates.evidenceGap: The soil-temperature band comes from Japanese T. matsutake shiro studies cited in the source, not from western T. murrillianum measurements; it is labelled provisional in the model provenance.
missing: stand age and understory composition (published but not representable)
coarse woody debris and substrate mineralogy
a western T. murrillianum thermal curve
published numeric drainage or available-water responses

candidates.why: The core Pacific Northwest chanterelle, named in PNW-GTR-576 as C. formosus and explicitly separated from European C. cibarius; abundant in Douglas-fir and western hemlock forests.
modelUses: mapped hemlock/Sitka-spruce and Douglas-fir host classes with smaller spruce/fir weights (source-supported hosts, engineering weights)
September-November core with a July-August shoulder from the qualitative midsummer-to-late-fall statement (engineering calendar)
maritime autumn rain band, wet-day count, rain recency and the autumn wet-up transition metric (engineering bands)
NLCD forest cover and canopy as forest-structure evidence, never as host identity

candidates.why: PNW-GTR-576 documents a distinct species apparently mycorrhizal with Douglas-fir and hemlocks, fruiting late summer to early fall in mature to old forests. Kept separate from the golden chanterelle because season and published stand association differ.
modelUses: mapped hemlock/Sitka-spruce and Douglas-fir host classes (same host weights as the golden chanterelle because the evidence does not justify different ones)
August-October core with July and November shoulders (engineering calendar from the source statement)
maritime autumn rain band and wet-up transition (engineering)
a declared evidence gap of 10 weight for the published mature-to-old-forest association, which cannot be obtained from the current GIS stack

candidates.taxon: Craterellus sp. neotubaeformis (Pacific Northwest winter craterelle / yellowfoot)
candidates.why: A separate PNW taxon concept from the European Craterellus tubaeformis (GTR-576 provisional name; Trappe 2004 found western/eastern/European populations genetically distinct). Trappe 2004 gives precise host and woody-debris evidence, and the winter fruiting window is a genuinely different phenology from every other modeled target.
modelUses: mapped hemlock/Sitka-spruce host class weighted heavily, with small Douglas-fir and fir/spruce weights (source-supported host, engineering weights)
November-March core with April and October shoulders from the published November-to-May window (engineering calendar)
broad winter precipitation band and wet-up transition (engineering)
a declared evidence gap of 20 weight for coarse woody debris volume/decay class and stand age, the strongest published drivers, which the GIS stack cannot obtain
candidates.evidenceGap: Trappe 2004 found well-decayed CWD was the substratum for 88 percent of sporocarps and that stand age and CWD volume were significantly related to occurrence, while slope, elevation and aspect were not. None of CWD, decay class or stand age is representable, so they lower confidence through a declared evidence gap and are stated in the user-facing reason instead of being replaced by generic canopy.
missing: coarse woody debris volume and decay class (declared gap)

candidates.taxon: Pacific Northwest king boletes (Boletus edulis complex)
candidates.why: A species complex with different hosts and seasons from Rocky Mountain Boletus rubriceps; no reconciled PNW species concept with host or phenology sources was located, and the Southern Rockies model must not be copied.
Colorado relevance was not established from sufficient primary evidence: forecasting would also require the host Russula/Lactarius fungus, and no Colorado host or season source was located.
Important western harvest group; regional taxonomy and northern season still need review, and no Southern Rockies source was located.

A distinct target from the PNW winter craterelle, which is implemented separately. Black trumpet taxonomy and phenology differ by region and no regional host or season source was located, so no generic all-Craterellus score is published.
Colorado oyster activity is riparian/urban and largely winter or shoulder-season, a different regime from summer mountain targets; substrate and season need a dedicated profile.
Do not map western puffballs to the existing C. gigantea observation ID; no primary Southern Rockies evidence was located in this pass.
Recognized harvest target; modern taxon, conifer substrate and season require a dedicated profile, and no Colorado source was located.
